# Vāseṭṭha Sutta (Snp 3.9 (PTS Snp 115))

**ID:** Snp 3.9 (PTS Snp 115)  
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Vāseṭṭha Sutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul2.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul2.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vāseṭṭha Sutta* (Snp 3.9, PTS Snp 115) is the ninth discourse of the Mahāvagga in the *Suttanipāta* [Anderson & Smith 1913]. Set in the Icchānaṅgala forest glade, the discourse opens in prose when two young brāhmaṇas, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, debate whether one is a true brāhmaṇa by birth (*jāti*) or by deeds and action (*kamma*), eventually bringing their dispute to the Buddha [Anderson & Smith 1913; Katre 1931; Collins 1993]. Comprising a prose narrative followed by 63 stanzas—forming the longest poetic ballad outside the *Pārāyanavagga* [Katre 1931]—the Buddha refutes hereditary caste hierarchy by appealing to biological taxonomy: whereas different species of plants, insects, quadrupeds, serpents, and fish possess distinct innate physical differences by birth, human beings share a uniform anatomy and lack fixed biological caste markers [Rahula 1956; Obeyesekere 2002; Chen 2014]. Consequently, caste designations are purely conventional names rooted in social occupation and human habit [Rahula 1956; Obeyesekere 2002]. The discourse culminates in twenty-seven verses that revalue the term "brāhmaṇa" by ethical action, each stanza ending with a refrain defining the genuine holy person through moral purity, non-attachment, and spiritual liberation [Obeyesekere 2002].

The two protagonists Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja also appear in the *Tevijja Sutta* (DN 13) and *Aggañña Sutta* (DN 27), forming a sequential narrative recognized in Pali commentary tracing their path from initial inquiry to monastic ordination [Collins 1993].

**Sources**

- [Anderson & Smith 1913] Dines Andersen and Helmer Smith (eds.), The Sutta-Nipāta (PTS, 1913) — Verified PTS text setting, placement in Mahāvagga, and textual opening.
- [Katre 1931] S. M. Katre, Early Buddhist Ballads and Their Relation to Older Upanishadic Literature (1931) — Noted the verse count (63 stanzas) and the core debate of birth (jāti) versus deed/action (kamma).
- [Rahula 1956] Walpola Rahula, History of Buddhism in Ceylon: The Anuradhapura Period (1956) — Described the discourse's biological argument comparing plants and animals with human equality by birth.
- [Obeyesekere 2002] Gananath Obeyesekere, Imagining Karma: Ethical Transformation in Amerindian, Buddhist, and Greek Rebirth (2002) — Analyzed the 27 ethical stanzas with the refrain redefining the brāhmaṇa and the critique of conventional lineage markers.
- [Collins 1993] Steven Collins, 'The Discourse on What is Primary (Aggañña Sutta): An Annotated Translation' (1993) — Detailed the interlocutors Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja and their narrative progression across DN 13, MN 98/Snp 3.9, and DN 27.
- [Chen 2014] Shuman Chen, Liberation of Matter: Examining Jingxi Zhanran’s Philosophy of Buddha-Nature of Insentient Beings in Tiantai Buddhism (2014) — Noted the text's categorization of plants and herbs among living beings (pāṇa).
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II: Buddhist Literature and Jaina Literature (1933) — Discussed the textual duplication between Majjhimanikāya and Suttanipāta.
- [McTighe 2001] McTighe, Mentoring in the Majjhima Nikaya — Observed the poetic duplication of the discourse in both Majjhima Nikāya and Suttanipāta.
